homePage.paragraph1: The number of officially recognized political prisoners in Belarus currently reaches more than {0} people.

paragraph2.content: {0} to create portraits of each illegally convicted citizen using the traditional Belarusian embroidery technique of red thread on a white background, thereby recording an important era of Belarusian history with a folk code - ornament.

paragraph3.content: {0} is a gesture of creative solidarity, allowing individuals to symbolically support those affected by the state regime and share their stories through the non-traditional tool of political protest - cross-stitching.

homePage.paragraph4: The embroidery process is a long and meditative experience that allows participants to concentrate on their thoughts and feelings for a particular arrestee. By creating a portrait of a political prisoner, participants sacrifice a little time as an act of solidarity.
homePage.paragraph5: Already, more than 400 people around the world have become "ambassadors" of the project, stitching portraits of political prisoners individually or in groups. The final form of the project will be a collective canvas of all the embroidered portraits, symbolizing the intertwining of political events and human destinies.

paragraph6.content: The project is a continuation of the series {0}, created by Rufina Bazlova in 2020-2021, and is run by the Stitchit Collective. Through the #FramedinBelarus project, the collective creative process allows individuals to speak out against injustice and stand in solidarity with political prisoners in Belarus.

section2.title: How big does my embroidery have to be?
section2.paragraph1: Choose any canvases that you feel most comfortable working with. The size of the embroidery will depend on that image. Each job will be a little different in format - that's ok, we take this into account.

section3.title: How much fabric do i buy?
section3.paragraph1: You can use any fabric with a cross weave, or buy a special fabric for embroidery - Aida. To accurately determine the size of the fabric, you need to count 145 cells on the canvas. However, counting so many cells is too long and complicated, so we suggest counting 10 cells, measuring the distance with a ruler and multiplying by 14,5. To the result add about 5 cm on each side - this will be your final size.
section3.paragraph2: The fabric for the embroidery is called Aida. It comes in a different raster - the number behind the word Aida determines how many crosses fit in one centimetre. The smaller the number - the larger the cross. Usually it is sold in metres of 140 cm width. We've calculated in advance how much Aida fabric you might need in different widths - see the size chart:

section5.title: How to embroider?
section5.paragraph1: We suggest that you start in the middle of your embroidery. Fold the fabric in half twice - this is how you will find the centre of the fabric. The centre is also marked on the diagram. This is your starting point. Count off the number of empty cells from the centre to the beginning of the motif - this is usually the foot of the schematic man. Do the same on the fabric.
section5.paragraph2: Continue the work, counting the empty and filled cells. Follow the scheme. There is already a counted number of crosses in the most complicated places.
section5.paragraph3: Watch the informative video lesson. (inserted video).

section6.title: Work subscription
section6.paragraph1: Instead of the "YOUR NAME, CITY, YEAR" line, sign the final embroidery with your name or pseudonym. If you worked on the embroidery collectively, have everyone embroider their name/pseudonym. We enclose a Latin and Belarusian alphabet from which you will make up your signature. You can come up with your own font. It would be great if you could also embroider the place you are from, the date, or any other text. If you think your work should be accentuated by decorations, add them.
section6.paragraph2: Please don't be afraid to make mistakes - the embroidery does not have to be perfect, let it be ORIGINAL, be YOURSELF!

aboutUsPage1: Stitchit is an art group created in 2021 by visual artist Rufina Bazlova and curator Sofia Tocar. The group works on burning socio-political issues using the traditional technique of embroidery as a tool of resistance and dialogue. Stitchit involves different communities and individuals into the creation process and blurs the lines of authorship. Collective means all people, who take part in a project and activities organized by Stitchit.

newsPageArticle1Perex: The group exhibition "The little bird must be caught" presents a part of the project #FramedinBelarus on the 13th edition of the international contemporary art festival Survival Kit, which takes place inside an old bank building, in the heart of Dome Square (Pils iela 23, Riga) from 3rd of September to the 16th of October.

newsTheLittleBirdP7: The international contemporary art festival Survival Kit is one of the largest contemporary art events in the Baltics, taking place in Rīga annually. It was started in 2009 as a reaction towards the global economic crisis, calling for a consideration of various survival strategies within the changeable world of today. Every year, the festival is dedicated to a new and significant social topic. Abandoned Riga buildings are often used to hold festival events in order to draw attention to their future potential for development.
